facts.text: I got into the business of healing back pain because I had serious back pain myself as a young man.
I had serious back pain as a young man caused by a series of athletic injuries.
I got into chiropractic and related whole-body disciplines because nothing else worked for me.
I developed my own very different variations on familiar chiropractic practices over time.
I do not “pop” backs or do any of that.
I draw heavily on basic elements of chiropractic discipline, my reading of scientific literature, and my experience as a practitioner.
I grew up in a traditional medical household.
I fully expected to go to medical school and then into practice.
My grandfather was a medical doctor.
My father is a medical doctor.
My mom is a nurse.
My aunt is a nurse.
My uncle was a pharmaceutical salesman.
My grandfather performed surgeries, delivered babies, made house calls, and was a master diagnostician.
I grew up believing modern medicine could fix most things.
I revere traditional medicine and understand it better than most.
I believe traditional medicine generally isn’t great at curing back pain.
When I was a teenager, I thought I was going to be a professional skateboarder.
I took many falls while skateboarding, some of them pretty bad.
I did not become a professional skateboarder.
Before I could become a professional skateboarder, I became a very young man with extremely serious back pain.
When my back pain started, I went to regular doctors.
I had ultrasounds, MRIs, and blood tests for my back pain.
My doctors discussed possible causes including slipped discs, ruptured discs, pinched nerves, and maybe cancer.
My doctors could not fix my pain.
I became increasingly convinced that many conventional doctors didn’t really know a lot about my back pain.
In near desperation, I turned to chiropractors.
I found at least some symptomatic relief from chiropractors.
Those chiropractors did not teach me how to make fundamental changes.
Those chiropractors did not talk about changing my behaviors or suggest how to take control of my own health.
I decided to train in chiropractic because I wanted to dig deeper into the real causes and real treatment of serious back pain, which I believed involved behavior and behavioral change.
My education in chiropractic was a long and complex process.
I took guidance from a range of experts in chiropractic and other fields.
I developed my own analyses and my own approach to permanently ending back pain in my patients.
I had a second round of back pain long after I should have known better.
The time of my second round of back pain was seven years ago.
I was working part of the time on a very promising medical start-up venture during that second round of back pain.
For six months, I was absolutely obsessed with that medical start-up venture.
I worked regular ten- and twelve-hour days with few breaks for leisure or exercise during that period.
Most of the time during that period, I was bent over my computer.
One morning during that second round, I woke up at six and started to sit up to go to the john.
When I woke up at six, I was smacked by the most ferocious pain I’ve ever had in my life.
The pain was even worse than anything from my skateboarding days.
I was knocked flat on my back and could not budge.
Even when I was lying absolutely still, the pain continued at a fierce level.
If I tried to move, the pain was much worse.
I lived alone back then.
I was seriously scared during that episode and wondered if I was going to die.
I considered that it might be a ruptured disc.
I also considered that it might be some weird cancer somewhere in my spine.
I concluded that the triggering behavior was probably months of nonstop work bent over a computer.
I stopped doing what had caused the pain in the first place.
To ease the pain, I rolled onto my side to see if I could stand.
I told myself to tense my abdominal muscles a little and slowly pick up my left foot while lying flat in bed.
I set my left foot down and picked up my right foot while continuing to tense my abdominal muscles.
I walked carefully, very gently, in place while lying on my back and not lifting my feet very far for about five minutes.
I walked off the pain and eased what I believed was a particularly bad muscle spasm near my lumbar spine.
I engaged my core by tensing the muscles in my abdomen to support my spine and keep it still.
I rolled onto my side while keeping my lower back still and my abdomen braced.
I made it to my knees and then my feet while keeping my lumbar spine still and my core engaged.
I tried walking erect and could walk.
I walked back and forth across the room carefully keeping my core tight for quite a while.
For the rest of that day, I was very careful about how I moved and did no more than a little easy walking.
I expected it would take a week for my back to return to normal because the spasm was so strong.
In a week, I was moving and living normally.
I resumed my regular exercise regimen and stuck to it religiously.
I did not let the intensity of my work interfere with my exercise regimen ever again.
I did not sit at the computer for more than thirty minutes at a time without taking a break and walking around.
After that episode, the pain never returned.

events.text: My second round of back pain began seven years ago.
I woke up at six and experienced ferocious back pain while trying to sit up to go to the john.
I stopped nonstop work bent over a computer after concluding it likely triggered the pain.
I walked in place for about five minutes to ease the pain during the episode.
I expected my back to return to normal in a week after the strong spasm.
In a week, I was moving and living normally and resumed my regular exercise regimen.
